systems.title: 3D Printer
systems.subtitle: Building a vase one layer at a time
systems.summary: An open-frame FDM printer melts plastic filament and draws a twisting vase one thin layer at a time — and the flow physics decides how fast it can go.
overview: A fused-filament (FDM) printer is a hot-glue gun on a robot. A motor pushes a 1.75 mm plastic filament into a heated nozzle, which melts it and squeezes out a line less than half a millimetre wide. Three motors steer the nozzle so the line traces the outline of one slice of the object.

This printer is a bed-slinger: the heated bed slides front to back (Y), the print head slides left to right on a gantry (X), and two lead screws lift the whole gantry by one layer height (Z) when a slice is finished. Watch the bed and the head move together: their combined motion draws the curved, six-lobed wall of the vase.

Speed has a hard limit. The hotend can only melt so much plastic each second, its volumetric flow. Faster moves or thicker layers ask for more; past the limit the plastic leaves the nozzle half-melted and the layers do not bond. The settings below compute flow, filament use and print time for the whole vase.

controls.label: Print speed
controls.help: How fast the nozzle moves along the wall.

controls.label: Layer height
controls.help: Thinner layers look smoother but take longer.

controls.label: Nozzle temperature
controls.help: Each plastic has its own melting window.

steps.title: Slicing
body: Before printing, software called a slicer cuts the 3D model into hundreds of thin horizontal slices and writes each outline as G-code: a list of moves such as G1 X12.3 Y4.5 E0.08, meaning move here while pushing out this much filament.
This vase at 0.2 mm layers becomes 320 slices; the controller on the front reads them one line at a time.

steps.title: Heating up
body: The bed heats first, to 60 °C for PLA, so the first layer stays soft enough to grip the textured sheet instead of curling up as it cools.

The nozzle then heats to its window: PLA prints at about 190–220 °C, PETG at 225–250 °C. A thermistor in the heater block measures the temperature many times a second and the controller adjusts the power to hold it steady.

steps.title: The first layer
body: The first layer is pressed slightly into the bed so it spreads and sticks. Four orange knobs under the bed level it to within a few hundredths of a millimetre — paper thickness matters here.
A badly levelled bed is the most common cause of a failed print.

steps.title: Drawing a wall
body: For each layer the nozzle traces the outline twice to make a wall two lines thick. Because this printer moves the bed in Y and the head in X, every curve is the sum of two straight motions, coordinated by stepper motors that move in steps of a few micrometres.
The fan on the head blows on the fresh plastic so it sets quickly and keeps its shape.

steps.title: Layer change
body: When the outline closes, both lead screws turn together and lift the gantry by exactly one layer height. The next layer is laid on top of the still-warm one below and fuses to it.
The vase twists because each slice is rotated a little from the last, and it bulges where the outline grows wider.

steps.title: Flow limits
body: Volumetric flow is speed × layer height × line width. A standard hotend melts about 15 mm³ of PLA per second; flexible TPU only about 4, because it buckles if pushed hard.
Try raising the speed and the layer height together until the flow gauge turns red: beyond that, the printer would lay down cold, weak, under-filled lines.

systems.title: Bottling Plant
systems.subtitle: Rinse, fill, cap, label, pack: 30,000 bottles an hour
systems.summary: Bottles race round a rotary filler, each under its own valve for just a few seconds. Speed the line up and find the point where they start to leave half-full.
overview: A drinks bottling line can fill tens of thousands of bottles an hour without ever stopping. The trick is the rotary filler: a big turning table with a filling valve over every bottle position. A bottle is gripped by the neck as it joins the table, filled while it rides round about two thirds of a turn, and released before it gets back to the start.

Most fillers work by gravity. Liquid sits in a ring-shaped bowl above the valves and flows down into each bottle; how fast depends on the height of liquid above the valve, just as Torricelli worked out in 1643. Fizzy drinks need a counter-pressure filler: the bottle is first filled with carbon dioxide at the same pressure as the bowl so the drink flows in gently without foaming, then the pressure is let off slowly (the snift).

Around the filler, other machines keep pace: a rinser cleans the empty bottles, a capper screws on caps, a labeler wraps a label round each one, an inspection gate checks the fill level and rejects any that are low, and a packer drops them into cases.

controls.label: Line speed
controls.help: Bottles per hour. Faster means less time under each valve.

controls.label: Liquid head in the bowl
controls.help: More liquid above the valve pushes it out faster (flow grows with the square root of the head).

steps.title: Rinsing
body: Empty bottles are swept off the pallet layer by layer and stood upright on the conveyor. Inside the blue rinser they are turned upside down and blasted with jets of sterile water or air.
Clean bottles then queue at the filler, spaced exactly one valve apart by a screw-shaped timing feed and a star wheel.

steps.title: Filling
body: Each bottle is lifted against its valve and rides round with the table. The valve opens, the drink runs down the inside wall of the bottle, and a small vent tube stops the flow when the liquid reaches it, so every bottle fills to the same height.
At 30,000 bottles an hour this 72-valve filler turns about 7 times a minute, giving each bottle almost 6 seconds under its valve.

steps.title: Too fast
body: Push the speed up and the table turns faster, but the liquid still flows at the same rate. Each bottle now leaves the filler before it is full.
Raise the liquid head or slow the line until the time under the valve is longer than the time the fill needs.

steps.title: Fizzy drinks
body: Switch to Cola. A carbonated drink would foam out of an open bottle, so the valve first pressurises the bottle with CO₂, lets the drink flow in under pressure, then vents it slowly. That extra time is why fizzy-drink lines run slower, or need more valves.
Try Cola at 40,000 bottles an hour and watch the inspection gate turn red.

steps.title: Capping
body: A sorter bowl spins loose caps until they all face the same way and slide down a chute. Spinning chucks press a cap onto each bottle and screw it tight to a set torque, so it seals but can still be opened by hand.

steps.title: Labelling and checking
body: The labeler wraps a printed label off the reel round each passing bottle. Then a light beam (in real plants often an X-ray or camera) checks the fill height.
Any bottle that is too low is pushed off the line into the red reject tray, and the rest are packed six to a case.

systems.title: Chocolate Factory
systems.subtitle: From cocoa bean to wrapped bar
systems.summary: A complete bean-to-bar line: roast, winnow, grind, conche, temper, deposit, cool and wrap — and why chocolate must be tempered to snap.
overview: A chocolate bar starts as the bitter seed of a tropical fruit. Fermented and dried on the farm, cocoa beans arrive at the factory hard and sour. Eight machines, working one after another, turn them into the glossy bar that snaps cleanly and melts on your tongue.

Heat does most of the work. The roaster develops flavour; the melanger's granite rollers grind nibs so fine — under 20 micrometres — that the tongue cannot feel the particles; the conche stirs warm chocolate for hours to drive off sharp acids and coat every grain of sugar in cocoa butter.

The cleverest step is tempering. Cocoa butter can crystallise in six different forms, and only Form V gives gloss and snap. The tempering machine melts every crystal, cools the chocolate to seed new ones, then warms it just enough to melt all but Form V. Slide the working temperature and watch what goes wrong when it is out of the window.

controls.label: Working temperature
controls.help: The temperature the chocolate is held at after seeding. Keep it inside the Form V window.

controls.label: Roast temperature
controls.help: Hotter roasts darken the beans and push flavour from fruity to roasty.

controls.label: Line speed
controls.help: Each mould holds four 100 g bars.

steps.title: Roasting
body: Fermented beans tumble in a gas-heated drum at 110–150 °C for 15 to 40 minutes. Sugars and amino acids react (the Maillard reaction), creating hundreds of flavour compounds and the familiar chocolate aroma.
A rotating sieve in front cools the batch quickly so the roast stops exactly where the roaster wants it. Try the roast slider: the sight glass and the cooled beans darken as the temperature rises.

steps.title: Cracking & winnowing
body: The roasted beans are cracked into pieces called nibs. A stream of air from the blower lifts away the light, papery shells, while the heavier nibs fall through.
A cyclone on top spins the air so the shells drop out into the bin — they become garden mulch or animal feed — and the clean nibs travel on to the grinder.

steps.title: Grinding
body: In the melanger two granite rollers roll round a granite bed. Nibs are about half fat (cocoa butter), so as they are crushed they melt into a thick, dark liquid called cocoa liquor.
Sugar and, for milk chocolate, milk powder are added from the hoppers above. Grinding continues until particles are below about 20 micrometres — smaller than the tongue can detect.

steps.title: Conching
body: The conche stirs and kneads the warm chocolate, 10 to 18 hours depending on the recipe. Aeration drives off volatile acids and water, and friction coats every particle in cocoa butter.
The result is smoother, mellower and more liquid. The name comes from the shell shape of the first trough, invented by Rodolphe Lindt in 1879.

steps.title: Tempering
body: Cocoa butter can set in six crystal forms. Only Form V is glossy, snaps cleanly and melts just below body temperature. The tempering machine first melts all crystals at 45–50 °C, then cools the chocolate to seed new ones, then warms it to the working temperature, which melts every form except V.

Each chocolate has its own window: about 31–32 °C for dark, 29–30 °C for milk and 28–29 °C for white, because milk fat interferes with the crystals. Too warm and the seeds melt: the bars bloom grey and soft. Too cool and unstable crystals thicken the chocolate.

steps.title: Depositing
body: A piston depositor fills every cavity of each mould with an exact dose, here 100 g per bar, four bars per mould. The moulds are polished polycarbonate, so each bar takes a mirror shine from them.
The moulds are shaken as they move on, which brings air bubbles to the surface so the bars have no holes.

steps.title: Cooling
body: The filled moulds ride through a tunnel chilled to about 12 °C. As Form V crystals grow, the chocolate contracts slightly, which is what lets the bars drop out of the moulds.
Cooling too fast or too cold causes condensation and sugar bloom, so the tunnel controls temperature and humidity along its length.

steps.title: Wrapping
body: Moulds are turned over and tapped; the bars fall out and the empty moulds return under the line. A flow wrapper folds gold foil and a paper sleeve around each bar.
The wrapped bars are counted into cartons. Store them at 15–18 °C: warmer, and cocoa butter migrates to the surface as fat bloom.

systems.title: Coin Mint
systems.subtitle: From a coil of metal to a pocketful of coins
systems.summary: A coil of alloy strip becomes coins: punched into blanks, rimmed, annealed, washed and struck between two dies with the weight of a hundred cars.
overview: A modern mint can make well over a million coins a day, and every one starts as a flat strip of metal rolled to the exact thickness of the finished coin. The strip unrolls from a coil into a blanking press, which punches a row of round discs, called blanks, with every stroke. What is left, a lace of holes, goes back to be melted.

The blanks pass through a rimming mill that rolls their edge up into a raised rim, then an annealing furnace that softens them at around 750 °C so the metal will flow into every detail of the design, then a washing drum that removes the dark scale left by the heat.

Finally a coining press squeezes each blank between an upper and a lower die inside a steel collar, with a force of 100 to 200 tonnes, in a few hundredths of a second. The metal flows into the engraved recesses of both dies at once and into the grooves of the collar, which form the reeded edge.

controls.label: Striking force
controls.help: Too little leaves the rim and lettering flat; too much wears the dies and squeezes out a flash.

controls.label: Press speed
controls.help: Strokes per minute. The animation is slowed so you can follow one strike.

steps.title: Blanking
body: The strip is fed forward one step at a time. On each stroke the orange press drives a row of hardened punches through it, and round blanks drop through the die below into a chute.
The blanks are packed in a staggered pattern, like the cells of a honeycomb, so about 80 % of the strip becomes coins. The holey leftover, the web, falls into the scrap bin and is recycled.

steps.title: Rimming
body: In the rimming mill a turning wheel rolls each blank against a grooved track, squeezing its edge inward and upward.
The raised rim protects the finished design from wear, lets coins stack neatly and helps the metal fill the edge of the die when the coin is struck.

steps.title: Annealing and washing
body: Punching and rimming harden the metal. In the furnace the blanks are held at around 750 °C, which lets the metal's crystals regrow and makes it soft again.
The heat leaves a dark oxide skin, so the blanks tumble through a washing drum with a mild acid and polishing media, then are rinsed and dried until they shine.

steps.title: Striking
body: A feed finger slides a blank onto the lower die. The ram drives the upper die down and, for an instant, the metal is under more than 3 billion pascals. It flows like thick clay into the engraved recesses of both dies and into the grooved collar around it.
The flat centre of the design fills first; the fine lettering and the tall rim fill last. Lower the force and watch them disappear on the coin above.

steps.title: Too hard
body: More force is not always better. Past about 1.25 times what the alloy needs, metal squeezes out between die and collar as a thin flash, and the dies crack far sooner.
Die life falls roughly with the fourth power of the overload, so mints set the force just high enough to fill every detail.

steps.title: Counting
body: Struck coins drop out along a chute into the counting bin. In a real mint they are inspected by cameras, counted by machine and sealed in bags or rolls.
At 600 strokes a minute one press makes 36,000 coins an hour.

systems.title: Container Terminal
systems.subtitle: Cranes, AGVs and the yard: the dance of a 1,800-box ship
systems.summary: Three quay cranes pluck containers off a ship, driverless AGVs race them to the yard and gantry cranes stack them. Add equipment and watch the bottleneck move.
overview: A container terminal is a factory whose product is a moved box. The ship is the incoming warehouse; the quay cranes are the machines that unload it; automated guided vehicles (AGVs) are the conveyor; the yard is the buffer; and the gantry cranes stack and retrieve. Every stage has a maximum rate, and the slowest one sets the tempo for the whole berth.

The choreography is exact. A quay crane lowers its spreader onto a container, locks the four twistlocks, lifts, trolleys the box over the quay and sets it on an AGV that has queued underneath. The AGV drives a fixed route to a yard block, where a rubber-tyred gantry (RTG) lifts the box into a stack. The empty AGV loops back for the next one.

Real terminals are measured in moves per hour and berth time. A big ship carries 20,000 TEU; a quay crane does 30–45 moves an hour; a terminal may run dozens of cranes and hundreds of AGVs. The interesting part is not any one machine but the queueing: a fast crane with too few AGVs simply waits, and a full yard slows everything behind it.

controls.label: Quay cranes
controls.help: Each crane can make about 33 moves an hour.

controls.label: AGV fleet
controls.help: Each AGV does roughly 17 round trips an hour. Too few and the cranes wait.

controls.label: Yard cranes
controls.help: Each RTG can stack about 50 boxes an hour.

controls.label: Vessel workload
controls.help: How many containers the ship carries. A bigger ship takes longer to turn around.

steps.title: The berth
body: A 1,800 TEU ship has tied up. The quay is a narrow strip between deep water and the yard, so every box must cross it in one direction and every empty vehicle must come back the other way.
The terminal operating system already knows which container goes to which yard block. It plans the discharge in a sequence that keeps the ship stable and the cranes from crossing each other.

steps.title: The quay crane
body: The ship-to-shore crane is a portal that straddles the quay. Its boom reaches over the ship; the trolley runs along the boom, and the spreader is lowered on steel cables to the container. Four twistlocks engage the corner castings, the spreader lifts, and the box swings clear.
One cycle — down, lock, lift, trolley, lower, unlock, return — takes about 100 seconds. At three cranes the quay can deliver roughly 100 boxes an hour, but only if the rest of the chain keeps up.

steps.title: The AGV shuttle
body: Automated guided vehicles are flat, low and battery-powered. They follow buried magnets or painted lines, and they never need a driver. An AGV waits under the crane, takes the box, drives to its assigned yard block and tips it onto a transfer stand.
The fleet is a moving queue. With eight AGVs and three cranes, the trips balance; cut the fleet to four and the cranes spend more time waiting than lifting. Switch to Flow to see the routes.

steps.title: Stacking the yard
body: Rubber-tyred gantry cranes straddle a block of containers and stack them four to six high. The yard is a buffer between the ship and the trucks that will take the boxes inland, so its density decides how long a ship can be discharged before the yard fills.
Each RTG can make about 50 moves an hour. Two of them are enough for three quay cranes; one is not. Watch the yard-fill gauge climb as the ship empties.

steps.title: Find the bottleneck
body: Four quay cranes can ask for 133 moves an hour, but four AGVs can only deliver about 67. The extra crane does not add throughput; it just adds a queue. The readout names the limiting stage: AGV.
Add AGVs until the quay is the limit, then add yard cranes. The best terminal is not the one with the most machines; it is the one whose stages are balanced.

steps.title: When the yard is full
body: A single RTG with a full yard becomes the worst bottleneck of all. Containers pile up, the AGVs queue, the quay cranes wait, and the ship's berth time stretches into days.
Real terminals avoid this with pre-stacking, rail links and a gate that keeps trucks flowing. A yard is not just storage; it is a scheduling problem.

steps.title: The automation layer
body: Above every machine sits the terminal operating system. It assigns each container a yard slot, each AGV a route, and each crane a sequence. It also decides when to stop a crane so a ship stays level and when to send an AGV to recharge.
Automation makes the choreography faster, but it also makes the bottlenecks more visible: a badly tuned fleet or a full yard stalls a line that never gets tired.

systems.title: DC Electric Motor
systems.subtitle: How current and magnets make motion
systems.summary: A demonstration motor turns as current meets a magnetic field. Raise the voltage, add load, and watch speed, current, torque and back-EMF balance out.
overview: Every electric motor, from a phone's vibration buzzer to a train, runs on one fact discovered in the 1820s: a wire carrying current in a magnetic field feels a force. Make the wire into a loop on a shaft and the forces on its two sides push in opposite directions — a twist, or torque.

A single loop would only rock back and forth. The split-ring commutator fixes that: every half turn, as the coil passes the vertical, the carbon brushes swap which end of the coil is positive. The current reverses just in time, so the torque keeps turning the rotor the same way.

A spinning coil in a field is also a generator. It produces a voltage that opposes the supply, called back-EMF, which grows with speed. That is why a motor draws a huge current when it starts or stalls, and why it settles at the speed where its torque matches the load.

controls.label: Supply voltage
controls.help: No-load speed rises in proportion to voltage.

controls.label: Load torque
controls.help: Like braking the shaft with your fingers. Too much and the motor stalls.

steps.title: Force on a wire
body: Current flows along the coil's long sides in opposite directions: away from you on one side, towards you on the other. In the field between the red north pole and the blue south pole, each side feels a force F = B·I·L at right angles to both.
The orange arrows show these forces: up on one side, down on the other. Together they twist the coil.

steps.title: The commutator
body: Watch the copper split ring at the front. Each half is wired to one end of the coil, and two carbon brushes rub on it. As the coil passes vertical, the gap in the ring passes the brushes and the connections swap.
The current in the coil reverses (see the yellow charges change direction), so the forces flip at the right moment and the turning never stops.

steps.title: Back-EMF
body: The faster the coil spins, the more it acts like a generator, pushing back against the supply. At full speed with no load, the back-EMF is nearly 12 V and only a small current flows.
Speed = (V − I·R) ÷ k: this motor runs at about 5,700 rpm on 12 V.

steps.title: Adding load
body: Brake the shaft and the speed drops, the back-EMF falls, and the current rises until the motor's torque (k × I) equals the load.
Push the load too high and the motor stalls: back-EMF is zero, current is limited only by the coil's resistance and the coil heats quickly — which is how motors burn out.

systems.title: Electrolysis of Water
systems.subtitle: Splitting water with electricity
systems.summary: A Hofmann voltameter splits water into hydrogen and oxygen, exactly two volumes to one, and proves Faraday's law of electrolysis as you watch.
overview: Water is two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen. Pass a direct current through water made conductive with a little salt, and those bonds are broken at the electrodes: hydrogen gas bubbles off the negative electrode (the cathode) and oxygen off the positive one (the anode).

The Hofmann voltameter, built by August Wilhelm von Hofmann in 1866, collects each gas in its own graduated column so the volumes can be read. There is always twice as much hydrogen as oxygen, because each water molecule gives two hydrogen atoms for every oxygen.

Michael Faraday showed in 1834 that the amount of gas depends only on the electric charge that has flowed: every 96,485 coulombs (one mole of electrons) frees half a mole of hydrogen. Switch to brine and the anode makes chlorine instead — the basis of a giant chemical industry.

controls.label: Current
controls.help: More current means more electrons per second, so gas forms faster.

controls.label: Time-lapse
controls.help: Speeds up time so the columns fill in seconds.

steps.title: Making water conduct
body: Pure water barely conducts electricity. A little sodium sulfate is dissolved in it: its ions carry the current through the liquid but are not themselves changed at the electrodes.
The three columns are joined at the bottom, so the liquid level in the central reservoir rises as gas pushes liquid out of the side columns.

steps.title: At the cathode
body: Electrons flow from the power supply into the negative platinum electrode. Water molecules take them: 4H₂O + 4e⁻ → 2H₂ + 4OH⁻.
Hydrogen bubbles rise and the liquid around the cathode turns alkaline — with universal indicator it goes purple.

steps.title: At the anode
body: At the positive electrode water gives up electrons: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻. Oxygen bubbles off and the liquid there turns acidic and orange.
Every four electrons make two hydrogen molecules but only one oxygen molecule, so the hydrogen column fills twice as fast.

steps.title: Faraday's law
body: Moles of gas = charge ÷ (electrons per molecule × 96,485 C). At 1 A for one minute, 60 C flow and about 7.6 ml of hydrogen and 3.8 ml of oxygen collect at room temperature.
The voltage needed is at least 1.23 V, the thermodynamic limit, plus extra overpotential to make the bubbles form quickly.

steps.title: Brine and chlorine
body: In concentrated salt water, chloride ions give up their electrons more easily than water: 2Cl⁻ → Cl₂ + 2e⁻. The anode now makes yellow-green chlorine, one volume for each volume of hydrogen.
Some chlorine dissolves, so slightly less than expected collects. The chlor-alkali industry uses this reaction to make chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide for plastics, paper and clean water.

systems.title: Four-Stroke Engine
systems.subtitle: How a spark turns fuel into rotation
systems.summary: A sectioned air-cooled single: watch the crank, rod and piston trade straight-line force for rotation while two cams open the valves in time with the spark.
overview: Almost every car, motorcycle, lawn mower and generator on Earth runs on the same idea, patented by Nikolaus Otto in 1876: draw in a charge of air and fuel, squeeze it, set it alight, and let the hot gas push a piston. Because each of those jobs needs its own trip of the piston, the cycle takes four strokes and two full turns of the crankshaft.

This teaching engine is cut in half so you can see every part move together. The slider-crank turns the piston's up-and-down motion into rotation. A toothed belt drives two camshafts at exactly half crank speed, so each valve opens once every two turns. The plug fires a few degrees before top dead centre, timed so that peak pressure arrives just after it, when the crank can use it.

Every number on the screen comes from one model: the true slider-crank geometry, sin² valve lift windows, a polytropic compression, a Wiebe burn curve and an exhaust blowdown. The indicator diagram traces the pressure against volume, and the area inside its loop is the work done each cycle.

controls.label: Engine speed
controls.help: The animation is slowed so you can follow it; the ×-gauge says by how much.

controls.label: Throttle
controls.help: Opens the intake: more air in, a bigger charge, a higher peak pressure.

steps.title: Intake
body: The piston falls from top dead centre while the cam on the left presses its bucket down and opens the intake valve. The falling piston lowers the pressure in the cylinder, and the atmosphere pushes a fresh charge of air and fuel in through the port.
The valve opened 10° before the piston reached the top and stays open 40° past the bottom, so the moving air keeps filling the cylinder by its own momentum.

steps.title: Compression
body: Both valves are shut. The piston rises and squeezes the 447 cc charge into the 45 cc chamber, a compression ratio of 10 to 1. The gas heats as it is compressed, and its pressure climbs from below one bar to about twenty.
Compressing first is what makes the engine efficient: the hotter and denser the charge when it burns, the more of its heat becomes work.

steps.title: Ignition
body: A few degrees before top dead centre the plug sparks. The flame does not explode at once; it spreads out from the electrode as a front, burning the charge over about fifty degrees of crank rotation.

Firing early gives the flame a head start, so peak pressure lands roughly 15° after the top, where the connecting rod has leverage on the crank. At high speed the spark has to come earlier still, so the gauge of spark advance rises with rpm.

steps.title: Power
body: The burning gas reaches its peak pressure, around 45 bar at full throttle, and drives the piston down. This is the only stroke that makes work; the heavy crank web and counterweight store some of it as momentum to carry the engine through the other three.
Watch the indicator diagram: the curve now runs far above the compression line, and the area between them is the energy delivered to the crank.

steps.title: Exhaust
body: Forty degrees before the bottom the right-hand cam opens the exhaust valve. The still-pressurised gas rushes out on its own, in a blowdown, and the rising piston then sweeps the rest out through the port to the silencer.
For a moment near the top both valves are slightly open together. This overlap lets the outgoing exhaust help draw in the next charge, and the cycle starts again.

systems.title: Fusion Tokamak
systems.subtitle: A star in a magnetic bottle, 150 million degrees hot
systems.summary: Twelve superconducting coils hold a glowing torus of plasma away from the wall. Heat it, fuel it and keep the magnets cold; push the density too far and the plasma disrupts.
overview: A tokamak is a doughnut-shaped magnetic bottle. Deuterium and tritium are heated until electrons separate from nuclei and the gas becomes plasma — a soup of charged particles at more than 100 million degrees. No material wall could survive that, so magnetic field lines curve around the torus and keep the hot plasma away from the vessel.

Fusion releases energy when a deuterium nucleus and a tritium nucleus combine into helium and a fast neutron. The helium stays in the plasma and heats it; the neutron escapes into a blanket, where its kinetic energy becomes heat. A steam cycle or a helium Brayton cycle can turn that heat into electricity.

The tokamak is a balance of four coupled systems: magnetic field, heating, fuelling and cryogenics. Field shapes the bottle; heating raises the temperature; fuelling sets the density; cryogenics keeps the superconducting coils at a few kelvin. Push one too far and the plasma cools, disrupts or quenches the magnets.

controls.label: Auxiliary heating
controls.help: Neutral beams and radio-frequency power heat the plasma; more heating raises temperature but costs electricity.

controls.label: D-T fuelling
controls.help: Pellet injectors set the density. Too much fuel at low field crosses the Greenwald limit.

controls.label: Toroidal field
controls.help: Coil current squeezes and stabilises the plasma; stronger field improves confinement.

controls.label: Cryogenic cooling
controls.help: Keeps the superconducting coils near 4 K. Too little cooling and they quench.

steps.title: The bottle
body: The vacuum vessel is a torus — a doughnut with a hole in the middle. Twelve D-shaped coils wrap around it and carry enormous currents; together they make the toroidal field that runs the long way around the ring.

A central solenoid drives the plasma current. That current does two jobs: it heats the plasma by resistance and it creates the poloidal field that twists the magnetic field lines into a helix. The twist is what makes a tokamak stable.

steps.title: Lighting the plasma
body: Neutral beam injectors fire energetic atoms across the magnetic field; they ionise inside the plasma and give up their momentum and energy. Radio-frequency antennas can also pump energy into the electrons or ions at a chosen resonance.

The plasma temperature is a balance between heating and losses. The alpha particles from fusion stay trapped in the field and heat the plasma from inside — self-heating is what makes a burning plasma different from a merely hot one.

steps.title: Holding the ring
body: Confinement time measures how long energy stays in the plasma. Stronger field, higher density and gentler turbulence all help; too much auxiliary heating can make the plasma harder to hold.
The product of density, temperature and confinement time is the triple product. Fusion needs all three at once — a hot but thin plasma, or a dense but cold one, will not burn.

steps.title: Fuel and the density limit
body: Fuel is injected as frozen deuterium-tritium pellets that fly through a guide tube and vaporise in the plasma. More fuel means more fusion, until the edge plasma becomes unstable and the discharge disrupts.

The Greenwald limit is an empirical density ceiling. Push past it and the plasma detaches from the wall, cools abruptly and dumps its stored energy into the vessel. Tokamaks protect themselves with massive armour and a fast shutdown system.

steps.title: Gain
body: Gain Q is fusion power divided by injected heating power. Q = 1 means the plasma releases as much fusion energy as the beams put in; Q = 10 is the target for ITER; Q = infinity is ignition, where alpha self-heating sustains the burn without auxiliary power.

A power plant needs more than Q. It needs the recirculating power — magnets, cryogenics, pumps, beams — to be a small fraction of the gross electricity. That is why engineering gain, not plasma gain alone, decides whether a tokamak is a power station.

steps.title: Cold magnets
body: The coils are superconducting: below their critical temperature they carry current with no resistance. Niobium-tin operates near 4 K, cooled by supercritical helium. A quench is a sudden loss of superconductivity — the coil resistance rises, the stored magnetic energy turns into heat, and the field collapses.
Cryogenics is invisible in the plasma but essential to it. Lose the cold chain and the machine loses the bottle; the plasma is gone long before the coils finish warming.

steps.title: Disruption
body: A disruption is a fast, uncontrolled loss of plasma current. The plasma cools, the current channel narrows, and enormous electromagnetic forces push on the vessel. Runaway electrons can drill through the wall.

Modern tokamaks predict disruptions and fire a shattered-pellet injection system to radiate the energy away safely. The goal is not to avoid every disruption; it is to make every disruption survivable.

steps.title: A power plant
body: The 14 MeV neutrons from D-T fusion are not confined by the magnetic field. They stream into a blanket, where they slow down and deposit heat; a lithium blanket can also breed tritium from the neutrons. The heat drives a steam turbine or a helium Brayton cycle.

A tokamak power plant is a chain of efficiencies: fusion power to neutron power, neutron power to heat, heat to steam, steam to electricity, minus the power that the magnets and beams consume. The plasma is the star, but the plant is the machine.

systems.title: Hard Disk Drive
systems.subtitle: Spinning mirrors that remember
systems.summary: With the lid off, watch the arm swing across spinning platters, wait for the right sector to come round, and read it — and see why seek time and rpm matter.
overview: A hard disk stores data as tiny magnetised regions on glass or aluminium platters coated with a thin magnetic film. A modern platter holds over a trillion bits per square inch, each region a few tens of nanometres across.

The read/write head never touches the platter. Air dragged along by the spinning disc lifts its slider into flight a few nanometres above the surface — like a jet flying a millimetre above the ground. A voice-coil motor, the same idea as a loudspeaker, swings the arm in milliseconds.

Reading a block costs two waits: the seek, while the arm moves to the right track, and the rotational latency, while the platter brings the right sector round under the head. At 7,200 rpm the platter turns every 8.3 ms, so on average you wait half a turn.

controls.label: Spindle speed
controls.help: Laptop drives spin at 5,400 rpm; server drives at 10,000–15,000.

controls.label: Requested track
controls.help: 0 % is next to the hub, 100 % at the outer edge.

controls.label: Slow motion
controls.help: Real seeks take milliseconds.

steps.title: Platters and spindle
body: Two platters, polished to a mirror, are clamped on a spindle motor that holds them at an exact speed. Data lies in concentric tracks — hundreds of thousands per surface.
Each surface has its own head, all mounted on the same arm, so they move together.

steps.title: The voice-coil actuator
body: Behind the pivot sits a flat copper coil between powerful neodymium magnets. Current through the coil pushes it one way or the other, swinging the arm — no gears, just magnetic force.
A servo uses position marks written on the disc to hold the head on the track centre within a few nanometres.

steps.title: Seek
body: To read a block the controller first moves the arm: it accelerates as hard as it can, then brakes, then settles on the track. Moving a third of the way across takes around 8 ms; to the next track, under 1 ms.
Pick a track and press Seek to watch the profile.

steps.title: Rotational latency
body: Once on track, the head waits for the right sector (pink) to rotate underneath. On average that is half a revolution: 4.2 ms at 7,200 rpm, 2 ms at 15,000 rpm.
This wait is why spinning faster speeds up random reads.

steps.title: Reading
body: As the magnetised regions pass, they change the resistance of a tiny magnetoresistive sensor in the head; the electronics turn those changes back into ones and zeros.
Outer tracks are longer and hold more sectors, so data streams faster at the edge of the disc than near the hub.

systems.title: Human Heart
systems.subtitle: Four chambers, four valves, one beat
systems.summary: A sectioned heart beats through the cardiac cycle: chambers squeeze, valves snap shut, blood flows, and an ECG traces the electricity that times it all.
overview: Your heart is two pumps side by side. The right side receives tired, oxygen-poor blood from the body and pushes it through the lungs. The left side receives fresh blood from the lungs and drives it out to every cell, around 100,000 times a day.

Each side has two chambers. A thin-walled atrium collects blood; a thick, muscular ventricle pumps it out. Four one-way valves keep the flow moving forward: the tricuspid and mitral valves between atria and ventricles, the pulmonary and aortic valves at the exits. Their closing makes the familiar lub-dub of the heartbeat.

This model is cut along the heart's long axis so all four chambers show at once. Everything moves to the same clock: the cardiac cycle traced by Carl Wiggers in 1915. Switch to Electrical to watch the impulse leave the sinoatrial node, pause at the AV node and race down the ventricles — the same wave the ECG records.

controls.label: Heart rate
controls.help: Resting adults run 60–100 bpm; hard exercise can exceed 170.

controls.label: Slow motion
controls.help: Stretch each beat so you can follow the valves.

steps.title: Two pumps
body: Blue blood returning from the body enters the right atrium through the superior and inferior venae cavae. Red blood from the lungs enters the left atrium through four pulmonary veins.
The thick wall between the two sides, the septum, keeps the oxygen-poor and oxygen-rich blood from ever mixing.

steps.title: Atrial kick
body: The beat begins at the sinoatrial node, the heart's natural pacemaker in the right atrium. Its signal makes both atria contract (the P wave on the ECG) and top up the ventricles with a last 15–20 ml.
Most filling has already happened passively; the atrial kick adds about a fifth, and matters most during exercise.

steps.title: Lub: valves close
body: The impulse pauses briefly at the AV node, then races down the ventricles (the QRS spike). The ventricles squeeze, pressure inside jumps above the atria, and the tricuspid and mitral valves slam shut — the first heart sound, lub.
For a moment all four valves are closed and the ventricles tense without changing volume: isovolumic contraction. Thin cords, the chordae tendineae, stop the valve leaflets turning inside out.

steps.title: Ejection
body: When left-ventricular pressure passes the 80 mmHg in the aorta, the aortic valve opens and about 70 ml of blood is thrown out; the right ventricle does the same into the pulmonary artery at a much lower 25 mmHg.
The left ventricle ejects roughly 60 % of what it holds — the ejection fraction doctors measure.

steps.title: Dub: relaxation
body: The ventricles relax (the T wave). Their pressure falls below the arteries, blood starts to flow back and snaps the aortic and pulmonary valves shut — the second sound, dub.
With all valves closed again the muscle relaxes further (isovolumic relaxation) until its pressure drops below the atria.

steps.title: Filling
body: The tricuspid and mitral valves swing open and blood that has pooled in the atria rushes into the ventricles. Then filling slows until the next P wave starts the cycle again.
Raise the heart rate: diastole shortens much more than systole, which is why a very fast heart can fill too little and pump less.

systems.title: Lungs & Breathing
systems.subtitle: Half a billion air sacs and a dome of muscle
systems.summary: Watch the diaphragm pull air into a tree of airways that ends in half a billion tiny sacs. Change your breathing or climb a mountain and see your blood's oxygen respond.
overview: Your lungs have no muscles of their own. Breathing in is done mostly by the diaphragm, a dome of muscle under the lungs. When it contracts it flattens and pulls down, the chest gets bigger, the pressure inside falls slightly below the air outside, and air flows in. Breathing out at rest is just the diaphragm relaxing and the stretchy lungs springing back.

Air travels down the trachea, which splits into two bronchi and then keeps branching, about 23 times, into ever narrower tubes. At the ends are around 480 million alveoli: air sacs a fifth of a millimetre across, wrapped in tiny blood vessels. Spread out, their surface would cover half a tennis court.

In each sac, oxygen crosses a wall less than a thousandth of a millimetre thick into the blood, where haemoglobin grabs it, and carbon dioxide crosses the other way to be breathed out. How much oxygen reaches the sacs depends on how much fresh air you move and on the air pressure around you.

controls.label: Breathing rate
controls.help: Breaths per minute. 12–16 is normal at rest.

controls.label: Breath size
controls.help: Tidal volume. The first 150 ml of every breath only fills the airways (dead space).

controls.label: Altitude
controls.help: Air pressure, and with it the oxygen you breathe in, halves by about 5,500 m.

steps.title: The diaphragm
body: Watch the red dome under the lungs. As it contracts it moves down by a centimetre or two, the lungs stretch to follow, and about half a litre of air flows in.
Breathing out at rest needs no effort: the diaphragm relaxes and the elastic lungs recoil.

steps.title: The airway tree
body: Switch to Airways. The trachea, held open by C-shaped rings of cartilage, divides into two bronchi. The right one is wider and steeper, which is why an inhaled peanut usually ends up in the right lung.
Each branch divides again and again into bronchioles, and finally into the alveoli where gas exchange happens.

steps.title: Gas exchange
body: The card below shows one alveolus beside its capillary. Oxygen is at about 100 mmHg in the sac and 40 mmHg in the blood arriving from the body, so it diffuses in. Carbon dioxide does the opposite, 46 mmHg in the blood and 40 mmHg in the sac.
Blood passes in under a second and leaves almost fully loaded: 97 % of its haemoglobin carries oxygen.

steps.title: Holding back
body: Breathe too little and carbon dioxide builds up in the blood, which turns more acidic. Oxygen in the sacs falls too.
It is rising CO₂, not falling oxygen, that makes you feel the urge to breathe.

steps.title: Up a mountain
body: At 5,500 m the air pressure is half that at sea level, so every breath carries half as much oxygen. Breathing normally, the oxygen in the sacs drops so low that the blood leaves the lungs far from full.
Now raise the rate and breath size. Breathing harder flushes CO₂ out of the sacs and makes room for more oxygen: the body does this automatically at altitude.

steps.title: Dead space
body: Fast, shallow panting moves plenty of air, but each 250 ml breath spends 150 ml just filling the airways and back. Only 100 ml of fresh air reaches the sacs.
Compare with slow, deep breaths: the same minute volume delivers far more fresh air to the alveoli.

systems.title: Injection Moulding Machine
systems.subtitle: How plastic toys are made in seconds
systems.summary: Pellets melt in a heated barrel, a screw shoots them into a steel mould under huge pressure, and a toy brick pops out every few seconds. Find the window between short shots, burns and warping.
overview: Most plastic things around you, from bottle caps to phone cases to building bricks, were made by injection moulding. It is the fastest way to make the same complicated shape millions of times with the same precision.

Plastic pellets fall from the hopper into a long heated barrel. Inside, a screw turns, dragging the pellets forward; friction and the heater bands melt them into a thick, glowing paste that collects in front of the screw. Then the screw stops turning and rams forward like a syringe plunger, forcing the melt through a nozzle into a closed steel mould at hundreds of bar.

The mould is kept cool, so the plastic freezes against its walls. A toggle clamp holds the two halves shut against the injection pressure. Once the part is stiff enough, the mould opens and ejector pins push it out, and the next cycle starts while the screw is already melting the next shot.

controls.label: Melt temperature
controls.help: Too cold and the plastic freezes before the mould is full; too hot and it burns.

controls.label: Injection speed
controls.help: Fast fills thin walls before they freeze, but too fast forces plastic out between the mould halves.

controls.label: Cooling time
controls.help: The longest part of the cycle. Too short and the part warps when it is pushed out.

steps.title: Melting
body: Pellets slide from the hopper into the back of the barrel. The turning screw has a deep channel at the back that gets shallower towards the front, so the pellets are squeezed, sheared and heated.
About two thirds of the heat comes from that shearing, not from the heater bands, which mainly keep each zone at its set temperature.

steps.title: Injection
body: When enough melt has collected in front of the screw, it stops turning and is pushed forward by the injection cylinder. A check ring on its tip stops the melt flowing backwards, so the screw works like a plunger.
Plastic fills the mould in about a second, driven by up to a thousand bar or more.

steps.title: Holding and cooling
body: Plastic shrinks as it cools, so the screw keeps pushing for a moment (holding pressure) to pack in a little more.
Then the part must cool until it is stiff. Cooling time grows with the square of the wall thickness: a part twice as thick needs four times as long. Water channels in the mould carry the heat away.

steps.title: Clamp and eject
body: The two links of the toggle clamp straighten as the mould closes, like locking your knee. That multiplies the force of the clamp cylinder many times and locks the mould against the injection pressure.
When the mould opens, ejector pins push the part free and it drops into the bin.

steps.title: Short shot
body: Too cold, or too slow, and the melt freezes at the thin edges before the cavity is full. You get a short shot: a part with missing pieces, shown grey in the bin.
Warm it up or inject faster and the full part comes back.

steps.title: Rushing the cooling
body: Cut the cooling time to speed the line up, and parts come out still soft inside. They bend as they shrink and the brick no longer clicks onto another.
Engineers balance cycle time against quality: every second saved is worth thousands of parts a day.

systems.title: Jet Engine
systems.subtitle: Suck, squeeze, bang, blow: inside a turbofan
systems.summary: A cut-away airliner engine: a giant fan, 10 rows of compressor blades, a ring of fire at 1,300 °C and the turbines that drive it all. Open the throttle and follow the air.
overview: A jet engine works in four steps that mechanics sum up as suck, squeeze, bang, blow. The fan and compressor suck air in and squeeze it to more than thirty times atmospheric pressure. Fuel is sprayed into that hot, dense air and burned. The expanding gas rushes out through turbines, which take enough power from it to drive the fan and compressor, and then out of the back.

Modern airliner engines are turbofans. Only about one sixth of the air goes through the hot core. The rest is pushed by the big front fan straight round the outside, through the bypass duct. Moving a lot of air a little faster is far more efficient, and much quieter, than moving a little air very fast, so the fan makes most of the thrust.

Two shafts run down the middle. The low-pressure turbines at the back drive the fan and booster on a long thin shaft; the high-pressure turbines drive the high-pressure compressor on a short hollow one around it. Each spins at its own best speed.

controls.label: Throttle
controls.help: From ground idle to take-off power.

controls.label: Air speed
controls.help: Flying fast means the engine must speed up air that is already moving, so thrust falls.

steps.title: The fan
body: The front fan, over 1.5 m across on a real engine, is the biggest single compressor stage. Its wide twisted blades push air backwards like a propeller in a duct.
Watch the blue particles: five out of every six go round the outside through the bypass duct. This engine's bypass ratio is 5.5.

steps.title: Squeeze
body: The air that enters the core passes ten rows of ever-smaller blades: three in the booster and seven in the high-pressure compressor. Each row speeds the air up and the fixed vanes between them slow it again, turning speed into pressure.
At full power the air leaves the compressor 32 times denser in pressure and over 550 °C hot, just from being squeezed.

steps.title: Bang
body: In the ring-shaped combustor, twenty nozzles spray fine kerosene into the compressed air, and it burns continuously. The gas reaches about 1,300 °C, hotter than the melting point of the turbine blades.
The blades survive because cooler air from the compressor flows through tiny holes inside them and over their surfaces as a protective film.

steps.title: Blow
body: The hot gas expands through the high-pressure turbine, which drives the compressor, and then the low-pressure turbine, which drives the fan. By the exhaust it has given up most of its heat as work.
What is left leaves through the nozzle faster than it came in. Thrust is mass flow times the change in speed: F = ṁ·(Vout − Vin).

steps.title: Idle to take-off
body: Push the throttle forward. The fan speeds up, the pressure ratio climbs, more fuel burns, and thrust rises steeply: from a few kilonewtons at idle to over 110 kN here.
Fuel per unit of thrust falls as power rises: the cycle is most efficient when the pressure ratio is high.

steps.title: In flight
body: At cruise the air already arrives at over 800 km/h. The engine must speed it up from that, so the same fan produces less thrust, and ram compression heats the air before it even reaches the fan.
At high altitude the thin air reduces thrust further, which is why airliners need such large engines for take-off and climb.

systems.title: Mechanical Watch
systems.subtitle: Keeping time with a spring and a swinging wheel
systems.summary: A coiled spring, a train of tiny gears and a wheel that swings eight times a second. Slow time down to watch the escapement let the watch tick, one half-tooth at a time.
overview: A mechanical watch has no battery. Its energy comes from a long steel spring coiled inside a drum called the barrel. Winding the crown tightens the spring; as it slowly unwinds it turns the barrel, and the barrel's teeth drive a train of wheels that turn the hands.

Left alone, the spring would unwind in a fraction of a second. The escapement stops that. A balance wheel, held by a hairspring as fine as a hair, swings back and forth eight times a second. Each time it passes the middle, it flicks the pallet lever, which releases the escape wheel by exactly half a tooth and then catches it again. That is the tick you hear.

On the way past, the escape wheel tooth slides along a jewel on the lever and gives the balance a tiny push, which keeps it swinging. Because a balance and spring always take nearly the same time to swing, however big the swing, the watch keeps time.

controls.label: Slow motion
controls.help: The real balance swings 4 times a second each way, too fast to follow.

controls.label: Mainspring wind
controls.help: A fully wound spring swings the balance wider. Near empty, the swing shrinks and the rate drifts.

controls.label: Regulator
controls.help: Moves two pins along the hairspring to change its working length: + makes the watch faster.

steps.title: Stored energy
body: The brass barrel on the left holds the mainspring. Wound up, the spring wraps tightly round the central arbor; as it runs down it relaxes outward against the barrel wall. Drag the wind slider down to see it.
A full wind here lasts 42 hours. The barrel turns once about every 8 hours.

steps.title: The gear train
body: The barrel's teeth drive the small pinion of the centre wheel, which turns once an hour and carries the minute hand. Each following pair of wheel and pinion speeds things up: the third wheel, then the fourth wheel, which turns once a minute and carries the seconds hand, then the steel escape wheel.
Every gear step trades force for speed, so the strong slow pull of the spring becomes a faint fast turn at the escapement.

steps.title: The escapement
body: The pallet lever rocks between two banking pins. Its two red jewels, the pallet stones, take turns blocking the escape wheel's teeth.

When the balance swings through the middle, its impulse jewel knocks the lever over. One stone lets go, the wheel jumps half a tooth, and the other stone catches the next tooth. Watch the gear train move in little jumps, one per tick.

steps.title: The balance
body: The gold balance wheel and the blue hairspring are the watch's timekeeper, like a pendulum you can wear. Their period depends only on the wheel's inertia and the spring's stiffness: T = 2π√(I/κ).
This balance beats 28,800 times an hour: 4 full swings each way per second.

steps.title: Regulating
body: The regulator arm on the balance cock moves two tiny pins along the hairspring. Shortening its working length makes it stiffer, so the balance swings faster and the watch gains.
A change of only 0.05 % in length moves the rate by about 20 seconds a day. Good watches keep within a few seconds a day.

steps.title: Running down
body: As the mainspring runs down, it pushes less, so the balance swings through a smaller arc. In theory the period would not change, but small errors in a real escapement make the watch run fast at low amplitude.
That is why watchmakers want a flat torque curve, and why a nearly empty watch keeps worse time.

systems.title: Nuclear Power Plant
systems.subtitle: Fission, steam and the grid — one coupled machine
systems.summary: A pressurised-water reactor in cut-away: split atoms in the core, follow the heat through the steam generator, spin the turbine, and meet the feedback loops that keep the chain reaction in check.
overview: A nuclear power plant is a steam engine whose fire never sees oxygen. Inside the reactor pressure vessel, uranium-235 nuclei absorb neutrons and split, releasing about 200 MeV each. That heat passes through a closed primary loop of water at 155 bar, so hot that it cannot boil, into a steam generator. There the heat makes steam in a separate secondary loop, and the steam drives a turbine and generator.

The chain reaction is controlled by a delicate balance. About 0.65 % of the neutrons are released not immediately but seconds later by decaying fission products; these delayed neutrons make a reactor controllable at all. Control rods absorb neutrons, and the fuel and water push back on their own: heat the fuel and the reaction slows (the Doppler effect), heat the water and it slows too. The reactor is designed to be self-correcting.

Two slow feedbacks matter most. Iodine-135 decays into xenon-135, a voracious neutron absorber. At power, xenon is burned up as fast as it is made; after a shutdown it accumulates into a xenon pit that can prevent a restart for hours. And decay heat — about 6.5 % of full power at the instant of shutdown — keeps coming even after the chain reaction stops. That is why cooling and containment are the heart of nuclear safety.

controls.label: Control rods
controls.help: Pull the bank out to add reactivity; drive it in to reduce power. The SCRAM button drops it all the way.

controls.label: Turbine load
controls.help: How much steam the turbine admits. Low load raises steam pressure; too low and the relief valve opens.

controls.label: Cooling water
controls.help: Condenser cooling flow. Less flow means higher back-pressure, lower efficiency and a hotter cooling tower.

steps.title: Splitting the atom
body: A uranium-235 nucleus that absorbs a slow neutron splits into two lighter nuclei and releases two or three more neutrons plus about 200 MeV of energy. Most of that energy appears as the kinetic energy of the fragments, which heats the fuel pellet within micrometres of their birth.
There are 12 fuel assemblies shown here; a real 3,000 MW reactor holds about 50,000 fuel rods, roughly 100 tonnes of uranium dioxide enriched to 3–5 % uranium-235.

steps.title: A chain reaction on a leash
body: Each fission gives neutrons that can cause more fissions. If exactly one of them goes on to split another nucleus, the reactor is critical: the power is steady. Slightly more and it rises; slightly less and it dies away.

Control would be hopeless if every neutron appeared instantly. About 0.65 % are delayed by seconds to minutes, released by decaying fission products. Those delayed neutrons slow the whole response, giving operators and automatic systems time to act. Switch to Neutrons to see the flux in the core.

steps.title: Control rods
body: The rods are made of boron carbide or an alloy of silver, indium and cadmium, all hungry for slow neutrons. Driving them into the core removes neutrons from the chain reaction; pulling them out adds reactivity.

Let the power settle, then pull the bank back out a little at a time. The reactivity gauge shows that the fuel and water quickly cancel much of the change: this reactor has a strongly negative temperature coefficient.

steps.title: The primary loop
body: Water at about 155 bar and 300 °C is pumped through the core at several tonnes per second. The pressure is far above water's normal boiling point, so the coolant stays liquid and carries heat away without turning to steam inside the core.

The pressuriser on the left is a tall tank half full of water and half steam. Heaters and sprays hold its pressure steady; it is the shock absorber that keeps the primary loop from boiling when load changes.

steps.title: Making steam
body: Hot primary water flows through thousands of inverted U-tubes inside the steam generator. On the other side of the tube walls, secondary water boils at about 70 bar into steam at 285 °C.
The two loops never mix. That is the central safety idea of a PWR: any radioactivity stays in the primary loop, inside the containment building, while clean steam goes to the turbine.

steps.title: Turbine and generator
body: Steam expands through the turbine blades, giving up pressure and temperature as it spins the shaft. The generator turns that rotation into electricity: about 950 MW from 3,000 MW of heat, an efficiency near 32 %.

The exhaust steam is condensed under vacuum and pumped back to the steam generator. Drop the cooling-water flow and watch the condenser pressure rise: less vacuum means less power from the same steam, and the cooling tower plume thickens.

steps.title: The xenon pit
body: Iodine-135, with a 6.6-hour half-life, decays into xenon-135, one of the strongest neutron poisons known. At full power the xenon is burned away by the neutron flux as fast as it forms, so it sits at an equilibrium worth about 2.8 % reactivity.

Cut power and the burn-up falls immediately while iodine keeps producing xenon. The xenon gauge climbs, adding negative reactivity and pulling the power down further — the xenon pit. After a shutdown it can take 20–40 hours before the reactor can be restarted.

steps.title: Defence in depth
body: Three barriers stand between the fuel and the environment: the ceramic fuel and its zirconium cladding, the steel pressure vessel and primary loop, and the reinforced concrete containment. Each is designed to hold even if the one before it fails.

The last line is the operator and the automatic protection system. Press SCRAM: the rods fall in under gravity in a couple of seconds, the chain reaction stops and the turbine trips off the grid. Decay heat does not stop, so the pumps, steam generator and relief valve must keep removing it. Try a SCRAM, then watch the fuel temperature and steam pressure.

parts.name: Containment
parts.role: A steel-lined, reinforced-concrete shell that holds the whole primary loop and can contain steam and radioactivity even in an accident.

parts.name: Reactor pressure vessel
parts.role: A forged steel vessel about 12 m tall and 4 m across, holding the core at 155 bar.

parts.name: Reactor core

parts.name: Fuel assemblies

systems.title: Oil Refinery
systems.subtitle: Splitting crude oil by boiling point
systems.summary: A tall column sorts crude oil into gas, petrol, kerosene, diesel and tar by boiling point. Turn up the furnace or switch to a heavy crude and see the barrel change.
overview: Crude oil is a mixture of thousands of hydrocarbons, from tiny molecules like propane to huge ones with fifty or more carbon atoms. Small molecules boil at low temperatures and big ones at high temperatures, so heating crude and letting the vapour cool step by step sorts the molecules by size. This is fractional distillation.

In a refinery, crude is pumped through a furnace and heated to about 360 °C. Most of it turns to vapour and enters the bottom of a column up to 60 m tall, filled with trays. The vapour rises, bubbling through liquid on each tray and cooling as it goes. Each product condenses on the trays where the temperature matches its boiling range and is drawn off there: diesel lower down, kerosene above it, petrol near the top. Gases leave from the very top.

What never boils, the heavy residue, collects at the bottom. Different crudes give very different mixtures: a light crude is rich in petrol and diesel, a heavy crude yields mostly heavy oils and bitumen.

controls.label: Furnace outlet
controls.help: Hotter vaporises more, but above ~400 °C the molecules start to crack and form coke.

controls.label: Throughput
controls.help: Thousands of barrels of crude a day (one barrel is 159 litres).

steps.title: Heating the crude
body: Crude from the storage tank is pumped through heat exchangers (not shown) and then the fired furnace, where it flows through tubes past burner flames. It leaves at about 360 °C, partly boiling, and rushes into the bottom of the column.
Heating 150,000 barrels a day takes over 100 megawatts, about as much as a small town uses.

steps.title: The column
body: The column is cut open to show its trays. Vapour (the dots) rises through holes in each tray, covered by bubble caps, and bubbles through a layer of liquid. Heavier molecules condense into that liquid; lighter ones carry on up.
So the column is hot at the bottom and cool at the top, and every tray holds liquid of a slightly different make-up: dark and heavy low down, pale and light near the top.

steps.title: The products
body: Each product is drawn off at its own height: refinery gas from the top (to the sphere), then petrol, naphtha, kerosene for jet fuel, diesel, fuel oil, and finally the residue from the bottom.
The card below shows the crude's boiling curve: how much of it has boiled away by each temperature. The coloured bands are the products.

steps.title: Heavy crude
body: Switch to heavy crude. Its boiling curve sits much higher: less than a fifth boils below 180 °C, and about half is still liquid at 360 °C.
Refineries that run heavy crude need extra units, like crackers and cokers, to break the big molecules into petrol and diesel.

steps.title: Too hot
body: Push the furnace higher and more of the crude vaporises, but above about 400 °C large molecules start to crack apart and form coke, a hard carbon deposit that clogs furnace tubes.
To recover more without cracking, refineries send the residue to a second column under vacuum, where everything boils at a lower temperature.

systems.title: Orrery: Sun, Earth & Moon
systems.subtitle: Why we have seasons and moon phases
systems.summary: A brass orrery turns through the year: Earth's fixed tilt makes the seasons, its slightly oval orbit changes its distance, and the Moon's position sets its phase.
overview: An orrery is a clockwork model of the solar system, first built in the early 1700s. Turn its crank and a gear train carries the Earth around the Sun once a year and the Moon around the Earth once a month.

The seasons are not caused by distance. Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January. They happen because Earth's axis is tilted 23.44° and keeps pointing the same way in space all year. In June the northern hemisphere leans toward the Sun: the Sun climbs higher and days are long. Six months later it leans away.

The Moon shines only by reflected sunlight, and half of it is always lit. Its phase is how much of that lit half we can see from Earth, which depends on where the Moon is in its 29.5-day trip around us. Move the latitude pin and the date to see daylight hours anywhere on Earth.

controls.label: Your latitude
controls.help: Positive is north of the equator. Jakarta is −6°, London +51°.

steps.title: The tilt
body: Earth spins around an axis tilted 23.44° from the plane of its orbit, and that axis always points toward the same place in space, near the Pole Star.
On 21 June the northern half leans toward the Sun. At 51° north the noon Sun stands 62° high and the day lasts more than 16 hours.

steps.title: Winter solstice
body: Half an orbit later the axis has not moved, but the Sun is now on the other side: the northern hemisphere leans away. The noon Sun at 51° north rises only 15°, and daylight shrinks to under 8 hours.
South of the equator it is summer. The seasons are reversed between hemispheres.

steps.title: Equinoxes
body: Twice a year, around 20 March and 23 September, the tilt points neither toward nor away from the Sun. Day and night are close to 12 hours everywhere on Earth.
At the equator the noon Sun is directly overhead on these days.

steps.title: Closest in January
body: Earth's orbit is a slightly stretched ellipse. It is closest to the Sun, 0.983 AU or 147 million km, around 3 January, and farthest, 1.017 AU, around 4 July.
That 3 % change in distance makes sunlight about 7 % stronger in January — yet it is winter in the north, which shows how much more the tilt matters.

steps.title: Moon phases
body: The Moon circles the Earth every 29.5 days from new moon to new moon. When it lies between Earth and Sun, its lit side faces away: new moon. Opposite the Sun, we see the whole lit face: full moon.
Halfway between are the quarters, when exactly half of the disc we see is lit.

systems.title: Pin-Tumbler Lock
systems.subtitle: Why only the right key turns
systems.summary: Slide a key into a sectioned brass lock and watch five spring-loaded pin stacks rise until every split lands on the shear line.
overview: Most front doors are held by a pin-tumbler lock, an idea patented by Linus Yale Jr. in the 1860s from a design thousands of years old. Inside a fixed brass shell sits a cylinder called the plug, and the key's job is simply to let the plug turn.

Five holes are drilled through the shell into the plug. Each holds a stack: a key pin at the bottom, a driver pin above it and a spring pushing both down. With no key, the driver pins straddle the gap between shell and plug and jam it.

The right key lifts each key pin by exactly its own length, so every gap between key pin and driver pin lands on the shear line at once. Then nothing crosses the gap and the plug can rotate. Try the wrong key: one or two pins line up, but the plug stays locked.

controls.label: Turn the key
controls.help: Only turns when every pin split sits on the shear line.

steps.title: Locked at rest
body: With no key in the lock, the springs push every pin stack down as far as it will go. Each driver pin now sits half in the shell and half in the plug, like a bolt dropped across the gap.
Try to turn the plug and the five driver pins shear-block it: that is why the dashed line between shell and plug is called the shear line.

steps.title: Sliding the key in
body: The key's tip is ramped, so as it slides in it lifts each pin stack up and lets it drop again into the cuts behind. You can feel this as the clicks of a key going in.
The cuts are called the bitting. This key's bitting is 3-7-4-8-2: the deeper the number, the deeper the cut.

steps.title: On the shear line
body: Fully inserted, each cut sits under its pin. Because every key pin was ground to match its cut, each split between key pin and driver pin now lies exactly on the shear line — the green dots.
With no pin crossing the line, the plug is free to turn and its cam at the back draws the bolt.

steps.title: The wrong key
body: A different key lifts some pins too high, pushing a key pin up across the shear line, and leaves others too low, leaving a driver pin across it. One misplaced pin is enough to stop the plug.
With ten depths and five pins there are 100,000 bitting combinations, though manufacturing rules reduce the usable number.

steps.title: Why picking works
body: No lock is perfect: the holes are never exactly in line, so under a light turning force one pin binds first. A lock-picker lifts that pin until it sets at the shear line, then the next, and so on.
Security pins with spool or serrated shapes, and tighter tolerances, make this much harder.

parts.role: Brass pins of different lengths, each matched to one cut of the right key.

Pulford, The Locksmith's handbook (2014)

systems.title: Refrigerator
systems.subtitle: A heat pump in your kitchen
systems.summary: A fridge does not make cold; it pumps heat out. Follow the refrigerant round its loop, open the door, heat the kitchen and watch the thermostat and the electricity bill respond.
overview: Heat always flows from warm to cold, so warmth from the kitchen is leaking into your fridge all the time through its walls and every time you open the door. A fridge keeps cool by pumping that heat back out, and the warm grid on its back is where it goes.

It does this with a liquid that boils at a very low temperature, the refrigerant. In the evaporator coil inside the freezer it boils at about −25 °C, soaking up heat as it turns to vapour, just as sweat cools your skin as it evaporates. The compressor squeezes that vapour, making it hot, and pushes it into the condenser coil on the back, where it gives its heat to the room and condenses back to liquid. A thin capillary tube then lets the pressure drop, and the liquid flows back to the evaporator, colder than ever.

A thermostat switches the compressor on when the inside warms past its set point and off when it is cool enough. Each joule of electricity moves about two joules of heat: the coefficient of performance (COP).

controls.label: Thermostat
controls.help: Food keeps best at 3–5 °C. Every degree colder costs a few per cent more energy.

controls.label: Kitchen temperature
controls.help: A hot kitchen leaks more heat in and makes the condenser work harder.

controls.label: Door open
controls.help: Warm air pours in and cold air falls out.

steps.title: Pumping heat
body: The fridge is cut open at the side and seen from behind. Food sits on glass shelves; above is the freezer, with the evaporator coil on its wall and a small fan.
Wait for the compressor to start: dots of refrigerant start to circle. Blue dots inside are cold and soaking up heat; red dots on the back are hot and giving it away.

steps.title: Boil and condense
body: In the evaporator the refrigerant is at low pressure and boils at about −25 °C. Boiling takes a lot of heat, which comes from the freezer air.
The compressor raises the pressure several times over. At high pressure the vapour is hot (red) and condenses back to liquid as it winds down the black grid, warming the air behind the fridge.

steps.title: The thermostat
body: The compressor does not run all the time. When the inside warms past the set point plus a degree, it switches on; once it is a degree below, it stops. The card shows the sawtooth this makes.
At 22 °C this fridge runs about a third of the time and uses about 0.6 kWh a day.

steps.title: Door open
body: With the door open, cold air spills out of the bottom and warm, moist air flows in at the top. The compressor runs much longer, and the moisture freezes on the evaporator as frost.
Frost insulates the coil and makes the fridge less efficient, which is why modern freezers defrost themselves.

steps.title: A hot kitchen
body: The hotter the room, the faster heat leaks in, and the hotter the condenser must get to dump that heat. The gap between the cold and hot sides grows, so each joule of electricity moves less heat: the COP falls.
Keep the back of a fridge clear and away from the oven, and it uses noticeably less energy.

systems.title: Robotic Assembly Line
systems.subtitle: Takt, welding robots and a car every minute
systems.summary: Bare car bodies index down a conveyor while articulated robots weld, a booth paints and a final station bolts on wheels. Change the takt or the robot count and watch the bottleneck move.
overview: A car body shop is a line of work cells arranged along a conveyor. Each cell performs the same set of tasks on every body that stops in front of it: framing, spot welding, sealing, painting, then doors and wheels. The line moves in steps, not continuously, because every station must finish before the next index.

The heartbeat of the line is the takt time — from the German Takt, a beat. If the plant needs 60 cars an hour, the takt is 60 seconds: one body must leave the last station every minute. Every cell is designed to finish inside that beat, and any cell that cannot becomes the constraint for the whole plant.

Welding is usually the constraint. A body-in-white carries around 4,000 spot welds, but a single robot cell only makes the 40–60 welds assigned to it. Robots work in parallel, so doubling the robots in a cell roughly halves its cycle; the conveyor, paint booth and final line do not speed up at all. This lab shows that balance: a fast conveyor with too few robots simply waits.

controls.label: Takt time
controls.help: The beat of the conveyor: one body indexes every takt. A shorter takt means a faster line.

controls.label: Welding robots
controls.help: Robots working in parallel in each welding cell. Fewer robots means a longer weld cycle.

controls.label: Batch size
controls.help: How many bodies this shift must build before the line stops.

controls.label: Mixed models
controls.help: Two body styles on one line add changeover time at every cell.

steps.title: The beat of the line
body: Five stations sit along one conveyor: framing, two welding cells, the paint booth and final assembly. A body enters every takt and stops at each station in turn. If a station is still working when the beat arrives, the whole line waits for it.
The takt is set by demand, not by the machines: 60 cars an hour means one car a minute, so the takt is 60 seconds. The plant is then designed so that no station needs longer than that.

steps.title: Framing the body
body: The skeleton arrives as loose pressings: floor pan, side frames, roof rails and bulkheads. A framing station clamps them into a rigid jig and tack-welds the first few joints so the body keeps its shape when the clamps open.
Everything downstream depends on this fixture. A body that is a millimetre out of square here will fight every robot, door and glass panel for the rest of the line.

steps.title: Welding in parallel
body: The welding cell has two robots, one on each side. Each robot swings a heavy spot-welding gun between programmed points, clamping two steel sheets and passing a current that melts a small nugget. A body needs about 46 welds at this cell.

With two robots each weld takes 2.6 seconds, so the cell needs roughly 60 seconds. That exactly fills the 60-second takt. Drop to two robots and the line is no longer limited by the conveyor — it is limited by welders.

steps.title: Where the queue forms
body: Speed the conveyor to 40 seconds and the two-robot cell cannot keep up. The body sits in the cell while the conveyor waits; the readout names welders as the constraint, and robot load pins at 100%.
Adding robots is the fix: four robots halve the weld cycle, six give headroom for a missed weld or a tip change. The conveyor is already fast enough; it was never the problem.

steps.title: Paint and final
body: The paint booth is a clean room on the line. The body is dipped in phosphate and e-coat, baked, then sprayed by robots inside a downflow of filtered air. Every speck of dust is a defect, so the booth runs at a slight positive pressure.

Final assembly is the least automated station: doors, glass, seats, wheels and fluids are still largely hand work. It is paced by the same takt, which is why the line cannot simply run faster than its slowest manual task.

steps.title: Changeover
body: Mixed-model lines build two or more body styles in any order. The robots carry several weld schedules and pick the right one from the body's radio tag, but clamps, grippers and fixture changes still cost time at every cell.
Turn on Mixed models: the weld cycle grows by seven seconds and first-time quality slips. The line can still run, but the cushion between the takt and the cell disappears.

steps.title: Balance, not speed
body: Eight robots bring the weld cycle down to 15 seconds, far inside a 45-second takt. Now the conveyor is the constraint again, and the robots spend most of each beat waiting — capacity you paid for but cannot use.
A balanced line keeps every station just under the takt, with a small buffer for variation. The goal is not the fastest robot cell; it is the highest output the whole chain can sustain.
