systems.title: Rocket Launch
systems.subtitle: Two stages, nine engines, eight minutes to orbit
systems.summary: A cut-away two-stage rocket flies a full launch: lift-off, max-Q, the gravity turn, staging and the push to 7.8 km/s. Load more payload and find out how much is too much.
overview: Reaching orbit is less about going up than going sideways. At 200 km above the Earth there is still gravity, almost as strong as on the ground; a satellite stays up because it is moving sideways at about 7.8 km/s, so fast that as it falls, the curved Earth drops away beneath it just as fast.

Most of a rocket is propellant. This one carries kerosene (RP-1) and liquid oxygen, which burn together in the engines. As the tanks empty the rocket gets lighter, so the same thrust accelerates it harder and harder. Rather than carry heavy empty tanks all the way, rockets drop them: the first stage burns out, falls away, and a smaller second stage carries on.

The best possible change in speed is given by the rocket equation, worked out by Konstantin Tsiolkovsky in 1903: Δv = Isp · g₀ · ln(m_full / m_empty). Getting to orbit needs about 9.4 km/s of it: 7.8 km/s of orbital speed plus losses to gravity and drag on the way up.

controls.label: Payload
controls.help: The satellite's mass. Every extra kilogram costs speed at the end.

controls.label: Time warp
controls.help: The real flight to orbit takes about eight minutes.

steps.title: The stack
body: The rocket is cut open down the front. The first stage holds orange kerosene below pale-blue liquid oxygen, which is so cold (−183 °C) that frost forms on the outside. A pipe, the downcomer, carries the oxygen through the fuel tank to the nine engines.
Above the black interstage sits the second stage with one large engine whose bell is shaped for vacuum, and the satellite inside the nose fairing.

steps.title: Lift-off and Max-Q
body: At lift-off the nine engines push with over 7,600 kN, about 1.4 times the rocket's weight, so at first it rises slowly. As it speeds up into thick air, the aerodynamic pressure on it climbs to a peak about a minute in: Max-Q.
Watch the exhaust plume widen as the air pressure around it falls.

steps.title: The gravity turn
body: A few seconds after lift-off the rocket starts to lean over. Gravity then pulls its path gradually toward horizontal, the gravity turn, so it builds sideways speed without ever turning against the air.
The flight path card shows the curve: steep at first, then nearly flat.

steps.title: Staging
body: After about two and a half minutes the first stage is empty. The stages separate, the first stage falls away, and the second stage's engine starts. Without the dead weight of the big empty tanks, the remaining propellant goes much further.
At about 110 km, above nearly all of the air, the fairing splits in two and falls away.

steps.title: Orbit
body: The second stage keeps pushing almost horizontally until the lowest point of the orbit is safely above the atmosphere, then shuts down. The payload is in orbit, circling the Earth every 90 minutes.
Δv left shows the rocket equation at work on the propellant still on board.

steps.title: Too heavy
body: Now try 22.5 tonnes. The rocket climbs on the same path, but the heavier second stage runs dry before it reaches orbital speed, and the payload falls back.
Because Δv depends on the logarithm of the mass ratio, a few extra tonnes on top cost far more than they seem to.

systems.title: Roller Coaster
systems.subtitle: Lift hill, loop and the forces that hold you in
systems.summary: A lift hill charges a train with potential energy; every drop spends it. Set the lift height, train length and dispatch interval, then watch the lap and the forces it produces.
overview: A roller coaster has almost no engine. A chain or a launch motor does one job at the start — lift the train to the highest point — and gravity does the rest. At the top the train has potential energy; at the bottom of the drop that energy has become speed. Losing height is the only way to gain it, which is why every hill after the first is shorter.

The track is a closed circuit: station, lift, drop, loop, a few airtime hills, a helix, then a brake run back to the station. The rails are steel tubes on a welded spine, supported by columns that carry the loads down to the footings. The train's wheels run on three sets of surfaces: running wheels on top, up-stop wheels underneath and side wheels against the rail, so it cannot lift off in a loop.

Riders feel the track through acceleration, not speed. At the bottom of a loop the seat must supply both weight and centripetal force; a 14-metre loop entered at 80 km/h pulls about 4.5 g. Too much and riders grey out, so designers shape the loop as a clothoid rather than a circle. Capacity is the other constraint: one train can only leave when it returns, so hourly riders are set by the slower of dispatch interval and circuit time.

controls.label: Lift height
controls.help: The highest point of the lift. More height means more speed everywhere else on the circuit.

controls.label: Train length
controls.help: Each car seats two riders. A longer train carries more people but adds weight and length.

controls.label: Dispatch interval
controls.help: How often the station sends a train. With one train, the circuit time becomes the real limit.

controls.label: Brake run
controls.help: How hard the final brake run slows the train before the station. Harder braking lengthens the lap.

steps.title: The lift hill
body: The train leaves the station and a chain dog catches under the car. The chain drags it up the lift at a constant, unhurried speed while the motor does work against gravity. At the crest the dog releases and the train is on its own.

Everything the train will do for the rest of the lap was paid for here. A taller lift means more potential energy, and therefore more speed at every low point — but also a bigger structure, a longer climb and a slower dispatch.

steps.title: The first drop
body: At the top the train is nearly stopped. Gravity accelerates it down the drop, converting height into speed: v = √(2gh) in the ideal case, with a little lost to rolling resistance and air drag.

The track curves through the bottom of the drop rather than kinking, so the change in direction is spread over time. That curve is what the rider feels as pressure in the seat: not speed itself, but the rate at which the velocity vector turns.

steps.title: The loop
body: A vertical loop is a centripetal-force machine. At the bottom the seat pushes up with the rider's weight plus mv²/r. With a 36-metre lift, the train enters at about 25 m/s and a 14-metre loop pulls roughly 5.5 g.

At the top of the loop the train is upside down and slower. If it is still moving fast enough, the seat still pushes; if not, the up-stop wheels catch the rail and the riders hang in their restraints. Modern loops are clothoids, tighter at the bottom and wider at the top, to keep the g-force humane.

steps.title: Airtime
body: A camelback hill is shaped so the train goes over the crest faster than gravity alone would keep it on the track. The up-stop wheels hold it down, but the riders feel the seat drop away — negative g, or airtime.

Airtime is the coaster designer's real currency. It is also a constraint: too much negative g and the restraints become uncomfortable and unsafe, which is why hills are shaped and trimmed rather than simply made steep.

steps.title: The brake run
body: After the last helix the train enters a brake run: magnetic or friction brakes squeeze the train down to station speed. The energy that was lifted into the train is now heat in the brake fins.
Braking harder is safer but slower, and every extra second on the brake run is a second the next train cannot be dispatched. On a one-train coaster, the brake run sets the capacity.

steps.title: Capacity
body: Eight cars carry sixteen riders. If the station could dispatch every 20 seconds, that would be 2,880 riders an hour — but one train cannot return before its lap is over, so the circuit time caps the real figure.
The readout tells you which limit you are on. Shorten the circuit, add a second train or load faster to raise capacity; making the lift taller usually lowers it.

steps.title: Designing the profile
body: Every hill after the first must be lower than the last, because energy is lost to friction and braking. A 42-metre lift gives a top speed near 95 km/h and about 6 g in a 14-metre loop — thrilling, but at the edge of what most riders tolerate.

The designer's job is to spend the energy where it feels best: a fast first drop, a smooth loop, a moment of airtime, then a controlled stop. The track is a budget of height, and every element draws on it.

systems.title: Orbital Life Support
systems.subtitle: A closed loop for air and water, 400 km above the ground
systems.summary: A cutaway habitat where electrolysis makes oxygen, a scrubber pulls CO2 out of the air and a water loop stretches every litre. Add crew, cut power or puncture the hull and watch the cabin drift.
overview: A spacecraft is a sealed world with a very small atmosphere. The International Space Station's habitable volume is about 388 cubic metres, and every kilogram of oxygen, water and food has to be launched from Earth or recycled on board. Life support is the machinery that keeps that sealed world breathable.

The core loop is simple to state and hard to balance. Crew members consume oxygen and produce carbon dioxide and water vapour. Electrolysis splits water into oxygen and hydrogen. A scrubber removes carbon dioxide from the cabin air; a Sabatier reactor can combine that CO2 with hydrogen to make methane and more water. Urine and humidity are distilled, filtered and returned to the water tanks.

Nothing closes perfectly. Filters clog, water is lost in brine, and power margins shrink when the station turns away from the sun. The controls here let you add crew, dim the solar arrays, tune the scrubber and tune the water processor; the gauges show the cabin atmosphere responding over the next hours.

controls.label: Crew aboard
controls.help: Each person consumes oxygen and produces CO2 and water vapour.

controls.label: Solar power
controls.help: Dim arrays cut electrolysis and scrubber power first.

controls.label: CO2 scrubber
controls.help: Removes a fraction of cabin CO2 each minute; needs power.

controls.label: Water recovery
controls.help: Urine and humidity processor. Recovery never quite reaches 100%.

steps.title: The can
body: The habitat is a pressure vessel with two decks. The outer shell keeps the vacuum out; the inner liner, hatches and feedthroughs keep the air in. The cutaway shows the machinery that stands between the crew and a very bad day.
Air is not still. Fans push it through ducts so carbon dioxide does not pool around sleepers and heat does not gather around electronics. The cabin is mixed, filtered and monitored continuously.

steps.title: Making oxygen
body: The electrolyser passes current through water and splits it into oxygen and hydrogen. The oxygen goes into the cabin; the hydrogen is either dumped overboard or fed to the Sabatier reactor. The stack needs water and a steady power margin.

The controller does not run flat out. It trims production to hold the oxygen partial pressure near 21.3 kPa — the same fraction of sea-level air that keeps a human conscious. Drop the power and the electrolyser is the first load to be shed.

steps.title: Pulling CO2 out
body: Four crew members add carbon dioxide to the cabin at a nearly constant rate. The scrubber — a packed bed of zeolite or amine — adsorbs CO2 as air passes through, then releases it into a vacuum or a regeneration loop.

The Sabatier reactor can combine CO2 with hydrogen to make methane and water. The methane is vented; the water returns to the tank. It is a clever loop, but it needs hydrogen, heat and another piece of machinery that can fail.

steps.title: The water loop
body: Water is the heaviest consumable on a station, so most of it is recycled. Urine goes through distillation, catalytic oxidation and filtration; humidity condensate joins the same stream. The product is clean enough to drink and to feed the electrolyser.

Recovery is never complete: brine, filter media and sampling take water out of the loop. The reserve gauge falls slowly even when everything works. Resupply ships top it up, and the crew learns to treat every litre as infrastructure.

steps.title: Add crew
body: Two more astronauts means more oxygen demand, more CO2 and more urine. The electrolyser ramps up, the scrubber works harder, and the water reserve drains faster. The cabin does not fail immediately; it drifts, and the drift is the lesson.
Watch the CO2 gauge first. It has the smallest buffer. Then watch the water reserve, which is the slowest variable and the one that limits how long the mission can continue without a resupply.

steps.title: A dim sun
body: At 40% solar power the arrays produce less than the habitat's baseline load. The power margin turns negative, the electrolyser stops, and the scrubber slows. Oxygen falls while CO2 climbs — two alarms from one cause.

Real stations manage this with batteries, load shedding and a carefully ordered list of what can be turned off. The model gives the life-support loads priority over comfort, but physics does not care about priorities.

steps.title: Puncture
body: A micrometeoroid punches a millimetre-sized hole in the shell. The cabin is not explosively decompressed — it is a big volume with a small leak — but pressure and oxygen partial pressure fall steadily. The crew has time to find the leak and seal it, if they know where to look.
Seal the leak and the pressure stops falling, but it does not come back. Repressurisation needs gas from a tank. The cabin remains at a lower pressure until the next resupply or a controlled repress.

steps.title: Closing the loop
body: The best operating point is not maximum power or maximum scrubbing; it is the point where every loop has a little margin. Run the electrolyser near demand, keep the scrubber above the CO2 production rate, and recover as much water as the processor allows.

A station is a system of systems. The air, water, power and thermal loops are coupled, and a change in one shows up in the others. That coupling is the engineering — and the drama — of living off Earth.

systems.title: Integrated Steel Mill
systems.subtitle: From iron ore to a glowing coil of strip
systems.summary: A blast furnace reduces ore into molten iron, a converter blows it into steel, a caster freezes it into a slab and a rolling mill squeezes it into strip. Follow the heat and find the stage that limits output.
overview: An integrated steel mill is one continuous argument with heat. Iron ore, coke and limestone are charged into the top of a blast furnace; hot air blasts in near the bottom and burns the coke, producing carbon monoxide that strips oxygen from the ore. The result is liquid iron at about 1,500 °C, which runs out of the tap hole into a ladle.

That iron is still brittle because it contains about 4% carbon. In a basic oxygen furnace, a water-cooled lance blows pure oxygen onto the melt; the carbon burns away as CO₂ and the iron becomes steel. The vessel tilts to charge scrap and pour, and the whole heat is finished in about 40 minutes.

The steel then goes to a continuous caster, where it freezes into a slab while moving, and to a rolling mill, where it is squeezed thinner and longer while still glowing. Every stage has a tonnage limit, and because the metal cannot wait around without cooling, the plant is really a chain of matched capacities. This lab lets you set the blast, oxygen, casting speed and mill load, then watch which one becomes the constraint.

controls.label: Blast volume
controls.help: Hot air through the tuyeres. More wind burns more coke and makes more iron, up to the furnace's limit.

controls.label: Oxygen lance
controls.help: Oxygen flow in the converter. It sets how fast carbon is removed from the heat.

controls.label: Casting speed
controls.help: How fast the slab is pulled out of the mould. Too fast and the core is still liquid.

controls.label: Rolling mill
controls.help: Mill load. The roughing and finishing stands can roll about 200 tonnes an hour at full load.

steps.title: The burden
body: The furnace is charged from the top with alternating layers of sinter, pellets, coke and limestone. A skip hoist carries each bucket up the inclined bridge and tips it into the bell, which seals the furnace so gas cannot escape.
The burden has to be porous: hot gas must rise through it while liquid iron and slag trickle down. Too much fine dust and the furnace chokes; too little coke and it cannot bear the weight.

steps.title: The blast
body: Stoves heat the blast to about 1,200 °C before it enters the tuyeres around the furnace's waist. The blast burns coke to carbon monoxide, and that gas reduces iron oxide as it climbs: Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂.

The furnace never stops. It runs for years between relines, with iron tapped every few hours and slag drawn off separately. The tap hole is opened with a oxygen lance and plugged with clay when the heat is out.

steps.title: The ladle
body: Molten iron runs down the runner into a ladle on a rail car. A full ladle holds 250–300 tonnes at 1,500 °C, and its refractory lining is chosen to survive the heat and the slag.
The car carries the ladle to the converter. On the way, alloy additions and a desulphurising lance may be used, because the steel's final chemistry starts here, not at the caster.

steps.title: Basic oxygen steelmaking
body: The converter is a barrel-shaped vessel on trunnions. Scrap is charged first, then the hot metal, and a water-cooled lance is lowered. Pure oxygen at supersonic speed burns the carbon out of the iron in a violent, bright reaction.

About 40 minutes later the heat is steel with less than 0.1% carbon. The vessel tilts to pour slag off one side and steel into a ladle on the other. Turn the oxygen down and the heat takes longer, which caps the whole plant.

steps.title: Continuous casting
body: The ladle pours into a tundish, which feeds a water-cooled copper mould. A dummy bar starts the strand, and the slab is pulled out while its skin freezes; secondary sprays finish the job before it is cut to length.

The caster's speed must match the steel supply and the metallurgical limit. Pull too fast and the liquid core breaks out of the skin — a breakout that stops the plant for hours. That is why casting speed is a hard ceiling in this model.

steps.title: Hot rolling
body: The slab is reheated and pushed through roughing stands, then finishing stands, each pair of rolls squeezing it thinner and longer. The strip leaves the last stand at more than 1,000 °C and is cooled by water sprays before it is coiled.

A coil can weigh 25–30 tonnes and be less than 2 mm thick. Rolling is the last chance to fix the steel's shape and surface, and it is also a capacity limit: if the mill is slow, the caster has to slow down or the slabs pile up.

steps.title: Finding the limit
body: With the caster at 1.2 m/min the strand can only take about 126 tonnes an hour, even though the furnace and converter can supply more. The bottleneck moves to the caster and the readout says so.

Raise casting speed and the mill becomes the limit; lower the blast and the furnace does. An integrated mill is designed so all four stages sit close to the same tonnage — the best plant is the one whose stages are matched, not the one with the biggest furnace.

systems.title: Volcano
systems.subtitle: Why some volcanoes ooze and others explode
systems.summary: A stratovolcano sliced through its summit. Change the magma's silica and gas, and watch gentle lava fountains turn into a 40 km column of ash.
overview: Deep under a volcano, rock melts into magma that collects in a chamber a few kilometres down. Being lighter than the rock around it, it rises through cracks and a central conduit toward the surface.

What happens when it gets there depends mostly on two things. The first is silica: magma rich in silica (like rhyolite) is cooler and millions of times stickier than silica-poor basalt. The second is dissolved gas, mostly water and CO₂, which comes out of solution as the pressure falls, just like the bubbles in a fizzy drink when you open it.

In runny basalt, bubbles escape easily and the lava fountains and flows away, as in Hawaii. In sticky, gas-rich magma the bubbles cannot escape. Pressure builds until the magma shatters into ash and shoots out at hundreds of metres a second, building a column that can rise into the stratosphere. Layer upon layer of lava and ash from thousands of such eruptions builds the cone.

controls.label: Silica in the magma
controls.help: Basalt about 50 %, andesite about 60 %, rhyolite over 70 %.

controls.label: Dissolved gas
controls.help: Mostly water vapour. More gas means more violent fragmentation.

steps.title: Inside the volcano
body: The volcano is cut in half through the summit. Far below, magma collects in a chamber. From its roof, a conduit leads up to the crater; other blades of magma have pushed sideways as a sill or squeezed up through cracks as a dyke.
The cone itself is built from alternating layers of solidified lava (dark) and ash and rubble (pale) from countless past eruptions.

steps.title: Runny lava
body: Basalt at about 1,200 °C flows like warm honey. Its gas escapes easily, so the eruption is gentle: lava fountains at the vent and rivers of lava down the slope.
These Hawaiian eruptions are spectacular but rarely deadly; you can usually walk away from the lava.

steps.title: Bursting bubbles
body: Add more gas to the same runny magma. Large bubbles now rise through the conduit and burst at the top, flinging out glowing clots of lava every few seconds.
This is Strombolian activity, named after the island of Stromboli, which has erupted like this almost continuously for over two thousand years.

steps.title: A plug of sticky lava
body: Silica-rich magma with little gas is too stiff to flow far. It piles up over the vent as a lava dome that grows like toothpaste squeezed from a tube.
Domes are dangerous: they can collapse or seal the vent until pressure builds beneath them.

steps.title: Plinian eruption
body: Sticky rhyolite full of gas. The bubbles cannot escape, the magma shatters into ash, and the eruption column shoots up tens of kilometres, spreading out as an umbrella cloud.

Hot avalanches of ash and gas, pyroclastic flows, race down the slopes at over 100 km/h. Lightning crackles in the column from the friction of colliding ash. Vesuvius in 79 AD and Pinatubo in 1991 erupted like this.

systems.title: The Water Cycle
systems.subtitle: Sun, sea, cloud, rain and river
systems.summary: An island diorama runs the water cycle: the Sun lifts vapour from the sea, wind carries clouds up the mountain where they rain or snow, and rivers and groundwater return it.
overview: The water you drink has fallen as rain countless times. Powered by sunlight and gravity, Earth's water moves in an endless loop between ocean, air and land — about 500,000 cubic kilometres of it every year.

Warm sunlight evaporates water from the sea surface. The warmer the air, the more vapour it can hold: about 7 % more for every degree Celsius, a law found by Clausius and Clapeyron. Wind carries this moist air inland.

When the air meets a mountain it is forced upward, expands and cools by about 6.5 °C per kilometre. Its vapour condenses into cloud droplets that grow until they fall as rain — or as snow above the freezing level. Rivers carry some of it straight back to the sea; the rest soaks into the soil and moves slowly through the aquifer below.

controls.label: Air temperature
controls.help: Warmer air evaporates more water and lifts the snowline.

controls.label: Onshore wind
controls.help: Pushes clouds from the sea toward the mountain.

steps.title: Evaporation
body: Sunlight warms the sea surface and gives water molecules enough energy to escape as invisible vapour. Over the oceans this happens on a vast scale: 86 % of all evaporation on Earth.
Raise the temperature and watch the vapour thicken. Saturation vapour pressure roughly doubles for every 10 °C.

steps.title: Clouds form
body: As moist air rises it expands and cools. When it reaches its dew point, vapour condenses on tiny specks of dust and salt into droplets about a hundredth of a millimetre across — a cloud.
Condensing releases the heat the Sun put in, which is what powers storms.

steps.title: Over the mountain
body: Wind drives the clouds inland until the mountain forces them up. Cooling squeezes out more water than the droplets can hold; they merge, grow heavy and fall. This orographic rain is why the windward slopes of mountains are the wettest places on Earth.
The far side, in the mountain's rain shadow, stays dry.

steps.title: Rain or snow
body: Air cools about 6.5 °C for each kilometre of height. Above the freezing level precipitation falls as snow. Drop the temperature and watch the dashed snowline creep down the mountain.
Snowpack stores water through winter and releases it in spring, feeding rivers when they are needed most.

steps.title: Back to the sea
body: Rain that hits the ground runs off into streams and rivers, or soaks into the soil. Below, it fills the gaps in a sandy aquifer and creeps toward the sea at metres per year — the cut face shows the groundwater moving.
A water molecule spends about nine days in the air, weeks in a river, but can stay thousands of years in deep groundwater or ice.

parts.name: Ocean
parts.role: Holds 97 % of Earth's water and supplies most of the evaporation.

parts.name: Sun
parts.role: The engine of the cycle: its energy lifts water as vapour.

parts.name: River
parts.role: Carries runoff from the mountain back to the sea.

parts.name: Forest
parts.role: Trees pull water from the soil and release it from their leaves (transpiration).

parts.name: Soil
parts.role: Soaks up rain like a sponge and lets it drain slowly downward.

parts.name: Aquifer
parts.role: A layer of porous sand or rock filled with groundwater, which flows slowly toward the sea.

parts.name: Bedrock
parts.role: Solid rock beneath the aquifer that water can barely pass through.

systems.accuracy: Evaporation scales with the saturation vapour pressure (Magnus formula); the freezing level uses a standard 6.5 °C/km lapse rate. Cloud growth, rainfall and flow speeds are illustrative, not a weather model.
